newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Canada's prima ballerina dances final tour.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Canada's prima ballerina dances final tour.

text.p: People stood amid a deafening roar of clapping, screaming and whistling as the curtain opened and a diminutive figure swept out to receive the wild applause of Canadian ballet fans.
Ballet aficionados and others are rushing for the chance to see Canada's prima ballerina, Karen Kain, dance the swan song of her 28-year career with the National Ballet of Canada.
The slight, dark-haired dancer was reflective, and giggly at times, in discussing her years with the National Ballet, where she has been the principal dancer since 1970.

"I was talented and I worked hard but I was also pretty lucky," Kain, 46, told Reuters in a telephone interview from her farewell tour, which ends in October. "I wasn't that easy to work with but I had a huge passion for what I do."

She said she was looking forward to being released from the physical pain of performing every night. "I have a sense of relief that I don't have to perform at this level anymore, but I also have a lot of sadness about it because I love to do it. I just wish it didn't hurt so much."

Kain's farewell tour is a showcase of four pieces ranging from traditional to modern dance, perhaps a glimpse of the many ways the ballerina has contributed to the world of ballet. Other dancers from the National Ballet star in the first three: "The Red Shoes," based on the Hans Christian Andersen tale, Tchaikovsky's "Pas de Deux," originally written for "Swan Lake," and "Herman Schmerman," a modern jazz piece.
EACH DANCE MARKS PART OF BALLERINA'S LIFE

Each dance figures as part of Kain's life. "Pas de Deux," for example, recalls how she stunned the ballet world in 1973 when she and partner Frank Augustyn won the best pas de deux prize at the Moscow International Ballet Competition.

Augustyn, Kain's friend and longtime dance partner, told the June edition of Canadian Chatelaine magazine that Kain was a hard-driving perfectionist who drove herself and others to meet her exacting standards. "I think now she's accepted the fact that achieving 100 out of 100 is impossible, but for a long time she had the drive to get to the 100 mark," he said.

The dancer who broke the stringent rules of the haughty ballet world by cutting her hair short and sneaking a puppy into the National Ballet School said her career choice had been a selfish one. "It consoles me sometimes to think that I've given a lot of pleasure to people but I know in my heart that I do it because I love to do it, not because I'm giving pleasure to other people."

The audience returns to the theatre after intermission for the last half of the show to find Kain on stage in front of a dressing room mirror dabbing her eyes and fretting over her hair as "The Actress," a ballet written for her by the National Ballet's artistic director James Kudelka.

Her movements are captivating and it is easy to see why the great Russian dancer Rudolf Nureyev called her "my angel" and why pop artist Andy Warhol sought to capture her image in 1980 with his screenprint "Karen Kain."

Two dancers stand out in the current production of "The Actress," as they did in the ballet world Kain inhabited. Early in the piece a dancer resembling Nureyev and later a young dancer bearing a remarkable resemblance to Mikhail Baryshnikov, who defected to Canada from the Soviet Union in 1974, appear on stage with Kain's character.

Kain said any resemblance to the two Russian dancers was strictly coincidental but she admitted that the message of dance, like beauty, was in the eye of the beholder. "That's not what it was meant to be. But you know what? It's like painting. You can see anything you want to see in the relationships and the people."

Despite offers from prestigious companies, Kain was committed to Canada's ballet troupe but she also danced with the famed Bolshoi Ballet, Le Ballet Nationale de Marseille, the Vienna State Opera, the Stuttgart Ballet, Makarova and Company and many others.

Despite all the accolades, Kain said she prefers to be anonymous offstage, when she goes shopping or has lunch with friends. "I'm not somebody who likes to be paid attention to when I'm in real life."

She said her 1994 autobiography, "Movement Never Lies," was written to deflect some of the overwhelming admiration and tell young hopefuls about the realities and hardships of the world she conquered.

"I guess I would want little girls not to idolise me too much. I'm just a regular person. I wrote a book (because) I wanted people to know that it's not all what it appears to be and that you should know what kind of a life it is that you're getting into."
